hook: Jonathan Ross started what became Google's Tensor Processing Unit as an internal side project, then left to found Groq in 2016, building a chip architecture designed purely for AI inference. Groq's language processing units made the company one of the most closely watched hardware challengers to Nvidia. In December 2025 Nvidia took a non-exclusive license to Groq's technology and hired Ross along with most of Groq's engineering team, a deal that returned billions of dollars to Groq's shareholders and moved its founder inside the company his chips were built to compete with. Ross now works at Nvidia as its chief software architect, and has spoken candidly about the leadership mistakes he made running Groq for nearly a decade.

standing.watch: The records leave the central question open: what happens to Groq after Nvidia licensed its technology and hired most of its engineering team, and what Ross builds at Nvidia under a non-exclusive license. No pending case against Ross or his companies appears here, and no listing or valuation event for Groq is recorded. The lawsuits on the site are monitored but show no development recorded yet by this tracker. Where the records are thin, they say less, and on Ross's own next steps they say very little.
standing.record: The record here is short and mostly one story: a founder who started what became Google's Tensor Processing Unit as an internal side project, left to found Groq in 2016, and then was hired back into Nvidia by the December 2025 license and hiring deal. Groq appears as his founded company, Nvidia as the public company where he is an executive. The lawsuits listed do not name Ross or his companies: the Grossinger matters concern Anthropic, and the Thomson Reuters case concerns Ross Intelligence, a different entity. The news stories naming him are largely unrelated to him on their face, covering payments, workflow, awards, government AI and drone acquisitions. The pattern that runs through the records is a career built on inference hardware, ending with the challenger absorbed into the incumbent.
standing.standing: Jonathan Ross now works inside Nvidia as its chief software architect, the company whose chips his own architecture was built to challenge. The records show he founded Groq in 2016 and built language processing units aimed purely at AI inference, making Groq one of the most closely watched hardware challengers to Nvidia. In December 2025 Nvidia took a non-exclusive license to Groq's technology and hired Ross along with most of Groq's engineering team, a deal that returned billions of dollars to Groq's shareholders. He holds no listed executive role at Groq in these records, and his influence now runs through Nvidia rather than through the company he founded.

quick_facts: Founded Groq in 2016 after leading the team at Google that designed and implemented the original Tensor Processing Unit.

Studied mathematics and computer science at NYU's Courant Institute, where he became the first computer science undergraduate to take PhD-restricted coursework in his second year, per Groq's own account of his career.
Groq's chips are called LPUs, language processing units, built specifically for AI inference rather than training.
On December 24, 2025, Nvidia announced a non-exclusive license of Groq's inference technology and hired Ross, Groq president Sunny Madra, and most of Groq's engineering team.
Now holds the title of Chief Software Architect at Nvidia.
Has said publicly that his early leadership mistakes cost Groq three to four years of progress.
